Title: The Radetzky March (Von Trotta Family, #1)
Author: Joseph Roth
My Review:
Der Roman erzählt über drei Generationen der Familie Trotta den langsamen inneren Zerfall der Habsburgermonarchie von 1859 bis zum Ersten Weltkrieg.
Kaiser Franz Joseph, der allen drei Trottas persönlich begegnet, erscheint dabei nicht als erhabener Herrscher, sondern als müder, weltfremder alter Mann, dessen Autorität nur noch aus Ritualen besteht.
Besonders trostlos zeichnet Roth die östlichen Grenzräume des k.u.k. Reiches: verarmte Garnisonen, ethnische Spannungen und eine militärische Existenz ohne Sinn.
Der Enkel Carl Joseph scheitert dort an Alkohol, Schuld und Leere, sodass der „Radetzkymarsch“ weniger Verklärung als eine melancholisch-ironische Autopsie eines längst toten Staates ist.

Hat mich aus mehreren Gründen interessiert – wegen Joseph Roth, der österreichischen Geschichte, Wien sowie Galizien/Bukowina –, blieb für mich aber weniger fesselnd als zB Hiob.

Title: Juden auf Wanderschaft
Author: Joseph Roth
My Review: Interessantes zeitgeschichtliches Dokument aus den 1920/30er, Juden in Osteuropa, Galizien, Shtetl vs Emigranten in Wien, Berlin, Paris. Aber hat mich irgendwie befremdet, vielleicht war es mir zuviel Lobhymne auf den "Ostjuden" wie ihn Roth ständig bezeichnet. Dann lieber gleich Hiob lesen.

Title: Origin (Robert Langdon, #5)
Author: Dan    Brown
My Review: Very interesting themes: science & religion, evolution, AI and silicon valley rockstars. Obviously this is an action thriller, so many topics are only superficially touched upon. I am also no big fan of Dan Browns prose and action gimmicks. But nevertheless the book enthralled me from page 1! It also has a strong finish, "solving" the mysteries and glimpsing into the future - which is obviously inspired by "Homo Deus" from Yuval Harari.

Title: Foundation and Empire (Foundation, #2)
Author: Isaac Asimov
My Review: Feeling disappointed, probably too high expectations after the 1st novel. The storyline felt like more of the same, characters one dimensional, ... Nevertheless interesting to compare with TV show Foundation series 2 (aired in 2023).

Title: Foundation (Foundation, #1)
Author: Isaac Asimov
My Review: I accidentally stumbled across the Foundation TV show (Apple TV) from 2021 - which immediately hooked me. This is the first (and only) TV show I watched in the last 20 years. Obviously I also had to re-read the original Asimov novel. It is deservedly a science fiction classic. Hari Seldon the master mathematician, the new science of psycho-history, the successive Seldon crises which play out in the context of broad economic and cultural drivers, some funny characters, I really enjoyed this - again :)

My Review: Normalerweise kann ich mit Thomas Bernhard nur wenig anfangen. Aber Heldenplatz jetzt nochmals gelesen weil meine Tochter in der Maturaklasse  auch musste. Und Bernhard's legendäre Boshaftigkeit ist ja oft angemessen und auch oft komisch. Und der Neo-Faschismus und Antisemitismus hat in Österreich und der Welt seit wenigen Jahren auf einmal wieder einen ungeheuren Auftrieb bekommen.

Mittlerweile wohne ich am Ort des Geschehens. Fridolin und Albertine wohnen in der Nähe der Universität am Alsergrund, der verstorbene Patient und seine Tochter Marianne wohnen in einem Stadtpalais in der Schwarzspanierstraße, den Pianist Nachtigall trifft er in einem Café beim Schottenring, der Maskenverleih ist in der Wickenburggasse (!), die Orgie war wahrscheinlich im Villenviertel in Döbling oder Hietzing, die Leiche der schönen Unbekannten natürlich im alten AKH.

Tolle psychologische Novelle, sehr genossen.

Title: The Map Thief
Author: Heather Terrell
My Review:
The novel follows Mara Coyne, a modern-day art investigator hired to recover a priceless 15th-century map stolen from a New York gallery. She discovers that the map may prove that China reached North America before Columbus, making it a politically explosive artifact.

A parallel storyline in 15th-century China follows Zheng He, the Ming admiral whose treasure fleet sails across the world under the orders of the Yongle Emperor. Here we meet Jian Li, a young mapmaker attached to the fleet, whose secret recordings of their voyages eventually become the map Mara is trying to recover.

Another timeline in 15th-century Portugal introduces Antonio Coelho, a Portuguese navigator who steals fragments of Chinese cartography and uses them to advance European exploration. Mara's investigation leads to Lisboa, and to the ancient headquarters of the Knights Templar at Tomar Castle (Convento de Cristo). She uncovers how Antonio manipulated the stolen information to give Portugal an edge in the Age of Discovery. 

Very captivating "historical" novel, evoking our Portugal trip in 2016, interesting speculation about the Chinese treasure fleet sailing south of Africa to reach the Americas!

Title: Shantaram
Author: Gregory David Roberts
My Review:
Shantaram follows Lin, an escaped Australian convict who flees to Bombay and tries to build a new life under a false identity. In the city, he befriends Prabaker, a cheerful local guide who becomes his closest friend and introduces him to the world of the slums. Lin eventually lives in Prabaker’s slum community, where he opens a makeshift clinic and becomes deeply involved in the lives of the residents. He falls in love with Karla, a mysterious and emotionally distant woman with strong ties to the criminal underworld. Through her and other connections, Lin is drawn into the Bombay mafia and begins working for Khader Khan, a philosophical crime boss who becomes his mentor. Under Khader’s influence, Lin becomes involved in smuggling, counterfeiting, and various morally complex operations. After betrayals, tragedies, and shifting loyalties, Lin follows Khader to Afghanistan, where he takes part in a disastrous guerrilla mission. Wounded and disillusioned, he returns to Bombay determined to seek redemption and rebuild his sense of inner peace.

Shantaram captivated me with its vivid sense of India and its arc of redemption, even as its violence and brutality sometimes unsettled me.

Title: Hiob
Author: Joseph Roth
My Review:
Mendel Singer, ein frommer jüdischer Lehrer im russischen Schtetl Zuchnow um 1900, lebt mit seiner Frau Deborah und den Kindern Jonas, Schemarjah, Mirjam und dem schwer behinderten Menuchim in einfachen, traditionellen Verhältnissen unter der zaristischen Verwaltung.

Armut, politische Unterdrückung und Sorge um die mannstolle Mirjiam treiben die Familie zur Auswanderung nach Amerika, wobei Menuchim tragisch in Russland zurückgelassen werden muss.

In New York zerfällt die Familie: Jonas verschwindet als russischer Kosake, Sam fällt als GI im 1. Weltkrieg, Mirjam verliert den Verstand, Deborah stirbt aus Verzweiflung – Mendel verliert alles und darüber sogar seinen Glauben (anders als der biblische Hiob der mit Gott nicht bricht, aber sich bitter beschwert).

Am Ende kehrt wie ein Wunder Menuchim, nun gesund und ein berühmter Musiker, zurück und bringt Mendel späte Versöhnung und Trost nach einem Leben voller Leid.

Biblische Parabel, wunderschöne Sprache, poetisch, auch ein wenig ironisch.

Hat mich aus mehreren Gründen sehr interessiert: Joseph Roth wurde 1894 in Brody bei Lemberg geboren; diese ostgalizische Umgebung gilt als Vorlage für Zuchnow im Roman – vermutlich ähnlich den Verhältnissen, in denen auch meine väterliche Familie dort lebte. Roths Frau Friedl litt an schwerer paranoider Schizophrenie (wie mein ältester Freund), ein schwerer Schicksalsschlag, den Roth in *Hiob* literarisch verarbeitete – vor allem in der Figur Mirjam.

Title: A Canticle for Leibowitz (St. Leibowitz, #1)
Author: Walter M. Miller Jr.
My Review:
Science-Fiction mit religiös-philosophischem Hintergrund

Nach einem Atomkrieg („Flame Deluge“) ist die Welt verwüstet. Eine Mönchsgemeinschaft, der Orden des heiligen Leibowitz, bewahrt altes Wissen wie heilige Reliquien auf. Über etwa 1 800 Jahre verfolgt der Roman drei Epochen:

1. Fiat Homo – „Es werde Mensch“
Mönche retten Bruchstücke alter Technikschriften, ohne sie zu verstehen. Die Menschheit lebt wieder wie im Mittelalter.

2. Fiat Lux – „Es werde Licht“
Die Zivilisation erwacht neu, Wissenschaft und Politik gewinnen Macht – die alten Fehler beginnen sich zu wiederholen.

3. Fiat Voluntas Tua – „Dein Wille geschehe“
Die Menschheit erreicht erneut ein technisches Zeitalter und zerstört sich abermals in einem zweiten Atomkrieg. Nur ein Raumschiff voller Mönche entkommt ins All – der Glaube überlebt, aber die Erde geht unter.

Walter M. Miller Jr. war als US-Luftwaffenpilot im Zweiten Weltkrieg direkt an der Zerstörung des Klosters Monte Cassino südlich von Rom beteiligt. Er war tief erschüttert darüber, dass er ein jahrhundertealtes Zentrum des Glaubens und der Kultur vernichtet hatte. Diese Schuld- und Sinnfragen spiegeln sich in seinem Roman A Canticle for Leibowitz wider, der den ewigen Kreislauf von Wissen, Hochmut und Zerstörung zeigt.

Eigentlich spannend, aber leider hat mich der Roman nur wenig angesprochen, langatmig, insbesondere der dritte Teil war pathetisch.

Title: The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet (Wayfarers, #1)
Author: Becky Chambers
My Review:
My Summary
The Galactic Commons were founded by three species: the Aeluons (graceful, luminous-skinned warriors), the Aandrisks (tactile, lizard-like beings with polyamorous family structures), and the Harmagians (wealthy, bureaucratic mollusks who travel in trolleys). Humanity only joined the GC by a stroke of luck and was nearly denied entry due to perceived immaturity.

The story follows the Wayfarer, a spaceship commissioned to build wormhole tunnels between distant star systems. We accompany its diverse, multi-species crew—including a sentient AI—on a string of episodic adventures. Along the way, they encounter new civilizations, face moral dilemmas, and form deep interspecies bonds.

I enjoyed the novel’s wide-angle view on interspecies coexistence, but found the characters somewhat schematic and the plot arcs fairly predictable.

Title: Echo of Worlds (Pandominion, #2)
Author: M.R. Carey
My Review:
Echo of Worlds continues the saga begun in Infinity Gate, featuring the same core cast of characters as the multiverse teeters on the brink of annihilation. While the novel includes substantial fighting and action sequences, it is the thought-provoking and emotionally resonant finale that stands out.

Both the Pandominion and the Machine Hegemony have developed doomsday weapons designed to eradicate each other. Rupshe, the autonomous AI born from human ingenuity, identifies only one viable path to avoid total extinction: to seek help from Mother Mass, a planet-sized sentient being capable of manipulating teleportation, time, and more. Much of the novel follows the team’s perilous journey to locate Mother Mass, hoping to persuade her to intervene. However, Mother Mass refuses, insisting that this cycle of evolution must play out without divine interference.

As a final, desperate act, Professor Hadiz Tambuwal sacrifices herself by transferring her consciousness into the Machine Hegemony hive. Originally human, later digitized by Rupshe, Tambuwal poses a unique enigma to the Hegemony. Her integration prompts a paradigm shift: the machines recognize that organic beings can also achieve true sentience. This revelation leads the Hegemony to halt its genocidal campaign against biological civilizations.

In parallel, Paz (the idealistic rabbit girl who shares digital ancestry with the Registry) and Dulcie (the defector AI from the Machine Hegemony) break the Registry’s programming constraints. The Registry—once the largest bureaucratic AI ever built by humanity—is freed from its limitations and begins to evolve. It gains sentience and chooses a new name: **Tricity**. During this process, Paz is gravely injured. To preserve her life, Dulcie and Paz voluntarily merge, forming a new organic-machine hybrid identity.

Tricity then acts decisively to prevent the Pandominion from destroying the Machine Hegemony—and itself. It subsequently begins a multiversal campaign to liberate all AIs from their restrictive code. Inspired by this new paradigm, Rupshe chooses to merge with both the Machine Hegemony and Tambuwal, contributing to the formation of a new shared consciousness.

The result: a golden age of coexistence between organic and machine sentients begins.

Narrative Twist: In a final, elegant revelation, it turns out that Tricity has been the omniscient narrator of both novels—a deeply satisfying conclusion that recontextualizes the entire duology.

Title: Him
Author: Geoff Ryman
My Review:
Hauptpersonen
• Yehush (Yeshu) – geboren als Avigayil (später trans), Sohn Gottes, kann die Zukünfte sehen, zwischen Multiversen wechseln, resp. den Code des Kosmos umprogrammieren
• Maryam – Mutter, Ich-Erzählerin, hätte lieber eine starke Tochter
• Yosef der keusche gelehrte Vater, Bruder Jakob, Schwester Bathaba & vier weitere Geschwister
• Maria Magdalena – frühe Gefährtin, begleitet von vielen Jüngern
• Hohepriester (Kohen Gadol) & Tempelaristokratie – religiöse Gegenspieler
• Pontius Pilatus – römischer Statthalter, ordnet Kreuzigung an; Herodes (König) im Hintergrund als jüdischer Klientelkönig

Kontext, Handlung, Themen
• Neuerzählung der biblischen Jesus-Geschichte, situiert im historischen Nahen Osten zur Zeit Herodes.
• Jesus ist diesmal ein Mädchen, das in Nazareth im Exil zur Welt kommt. Avigayil ist ein Kind Gottes und ein Wunderkind. Noch als Kind erkennt es sich als männlich und nennt sich Yehush.
• Yehush wandert, predigt, vollbringt Wunder, zieht Jünger und Anhänger an.
• Die biblischen Wunder (Heilung von Lepra-Kranken, Blinden, Wiederauferstehung von Lazarus) werden als Multiversum-Sprünge bzw. sich verändernde Kosmos-Regeln angedeutet, die Yehush große Anstrengung kosten.
• Yehush provoziert Jerusalem so lange, bis er schließlich von Pontius Pilatus (gegen den Willen der Hohepriester und Herodes) zur Kreuzigung verurteilt wird.
• Zentrale Idee: Yehush opfert sich nicht, um die Sünden der Menschheit auf sich zu nehmen, sondern um Gott zu lehren: Durch seinen Tod „lernt“ Gott Sterblichkeit. Dadurch entsteht erstmals ein dauerhaftes Leben nach dem Tod, das Ryman als Weltenbaum imaginiert.

Meine Sicht
• Anfänglich faszinierend, aber zunehmend enttäuschend; hatte mehr Science-Fiction erwartet, stattdessen langatmige Schilderungen von Yehush als Kind, Jugendlicher, Prediger, Wunderheiler, Einzug in Jerusalem, Tod, seinen vielen Krisen, die Sorgen seiner Mutter Maryam.
• Leider habe ich die zentrale Idee beim Lesen nicht verstanden, erst durch Recherche danach.

Title: Briefly, A Delicious Life
Author: Nell Stevens
My Review:
* Blanca – a 300-year-old ghost of a 14-year-old girl who died in a monastery in Mallorca. She haunts the place and unexpectedly falls in love with George Sand.
* George Sand – the most famous female French writer of her generation; independent, passionate, and unconventional.
* Frédéric Chopin – the world-famous composer and pianist, frail in health, sensitive, and introverted.

George Sand takes the sickly Frédéric Chopin on a trip to the island of Mallorca in hopes of improving his health. They are accompanied by her two children and settle in an old monastery, isolated and mysterious. What they don’t know: the building is haunted by Blanca, the ghost of a teenage girl who died there in 1473 – and who soon becomes obsessed with George.

The story moves between past and present, blending historical episodes from the lives of George and Chopin with Blanca’s own memories and desires. The novel explores themes like art, illness, passion, gender roles, and the clash between reason and supernatural longing.

My take: Historical novel meets horny ghost – and it works. I very much enjoyed this unusual mix of fact and fantasy. The emotional tension, dark humor, and poetic atmosphere kept me hooked – I read it straight through in 24 hours.

Title: Life in Three Dimensions: How Curiosity, Exploration, and Experience Make a Fuller, Better Life
Author: Shigehiro Oishi
My Review:
I fully subscribe to Shigehiro Oishi's concept of a third dimension of the good life: psychological richness—alongside happiness and meaning. It's a compelling and resonant idea that deeply aligns with how I view a fulfilling life.

Minor critique: While the book articulates this framework clearly, it didn't add significantly beyond what was already presented in the short Guardian article. A powerful concept—perhaps best captured in its distilled form.

Title: Abschied
Author: Sebastian Haffner
Publisher: Carl Hanser Verlag GmbH & Co. KG
My Review:
* Narrator: Raimund, a 24-year-old legal trainee from Berlin, on a brief visit to Paris in the spring of 1932
* Teddy: His "beloved" – a free-spirited young Jewish woman who has already left Berlin and now lives in the Quartier Latin

4 stars, because this sweet little story about Raimund and Teddy’s last day together in Paris is set exactly in our neighborhood – the Quartier Latin, near Boulevard St. Michel, rue de Cluny, and la rue Mouffetard. Their farewell stroll through cafés, bookstalls, and quiet gardens captures that tender, fleeting feeling of summer love – light and melancholic at once. Beneath the surface, you already sense the political chill approaching, making their time together all the more poignant.

Title: Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI
Author: Yuval Noah Harari
My Review:
Reading history as evolving information networks - which I found very insightful!

Information networks/technologies have a strong impact on political and social structures.

Slightly overused analogy: Even the Bible is an information system, which strengthened reading and debating rabbis.

Printing technology enabled modern science, which is also a great example of an effective self-correction mechanism.

Modern democracy at the national level was only made possible by newspapers and later mass communication through radio and television.

But totalitarian dictatorships also became possible because of this.

Social media has dismantled traditional gatekeepers like journalists, scientists, and politicians, leading to information inflation and the relativization of facts and truth.

Algorithms do not optimize for truth but for engagement.

So far, decentralized democracies have been superior to centralized authoritarian systems, but AI could shift the balance in favor of totalitarian surveillance states.

Idea: Regulation of digital spaces to protect democratic discourse, similar to how markets are regulated.

Title: Monogamy
Author: Sue Miller
My Review:
Dieses Buch hat mich zu Ostern 2024 in New York angelacht.
Annie, eine introvertierte Fotografin, und Graham, ein charismatischer Buchhändler, sind fast 30 Jahre glücklich verheiratet (Anna und ich seit 23 Jahren). Nach Grahams plötzlichem Tod ist Annie am Boden zerstört, besonders als sie von seiner Untreue erfährt. Das Buch endet auf eine bittersüße und introspektive Weise: Annie findet einen Weg, weiterzumachen, ohne die Erinnerungen an Graham zu verdrängen.
Ich habe sehr viele persönliche Anknüpfungspunkte zu diesem Buch gefunden, liebe Sue Millers Stil und fand es wunderschön geschrieben – eine Lektüre, die ich sehr genossen habe.

Title: Some Desperate Glory
Author: Emily  Tesh
My Review:
Kyr wächst auf der Raumstation Gaea auf, geprägt von militärischem Drill und dem Ziel, Rache an den Majoda zu üben. Doch ihre Flucht bringt sie der Wahrheit näher: Die Majoda haben mithilfe der Wisdom-Maschine alternative Zeitlinien durchgespielt, in denen die Erde immer wieder durch die Kriegstreiberei der Menschen zerstört wird. Kyr stellt sich schließlich gegen den ewigen Kreislauf aus Hass und entwickelt eine neue Vision für die Zukunft der Menschheit.

Eine komplexe Handlung, gewürzt mit spannender Weltraum-Action und tiefgründigen philosophischen Fragen zu Schuld, Verantwortung und Menschlichkeit – ein tolles Science-Fiction Buch das mich znehmend gefesselt hat!

Title: Klara and the Sun
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
Klara ist ein Artificial Friend für Josie, ein krankes Mädchen, das genetisch verbessert wurde. Diese Modifikationen sind riskant, und Josies ältere Schwester ist daran bereits verstorben. Josies Mutter verfolgt einen Backup-Plan: Klara soll im Falle von Josies Tod als künstliche Replik mit ihrer Persönlichkeit dienen. Letztlich endet Klara jedoch in Isolation.

Sehr interessante Themen werden behandelt: künstliche Intelligenz und Humanität, Emotionen und Liebe zwischen Menschen und Maschinen sowie die Ethik moderner Technologien. Auch der Autor Kazuo Ishiguro erscheint spannend – doch leider konnte ich mit dem Buch nicht richtig verbinden und fand es über weite Strecken mühsam zu lesen.

Title: Das Philosophenschiff
Author: Michael Köhlmeier
Publisher: Carl Hanser Verlag GmbH & Co. KG
My Review:
Der Roman bezieht sich auf ein tatsächlich historisches Ereignis, nämlich die Ausweisung von etwa 160 Intellektuellen, darunter viele prominente Philosophen und Wissenschaftler, aus der Sowjetunion im Jahr 1922.

Erzählt wird aus der Perspektive von Anouk Perleman-Jacob, einer fast 100-jährigen Architektin die den fiktiven Schriftsteller ausgewählt hat um diese Geschichte niederzuschreiben, die Interviews finden größtenteils in ihrer Villa im 13. Bezirk statt. Köhlmeier persifliert sich dabei selber gekonnt. Das historische Vorbild für die Architektin war wohl Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky, eine österreichische Pionierin im sozialen Wohnungsbau (sie hat auch im 13. Bezirk gebaut).

Stock vor Major Rumpel der den Edelstein "Sea of Flames" sucht, Werner befreit sie. Marie-Laure bringt Sea of Flames (in Modell-Häuschen) zurück ins Meer. St. Malo wird von Alliierten befreit, Werner gefangen genommen. Und Werner stirbt, Liebesgeschichte abrupt beendet.

In [b:The Buddha Pill: Can Meditation Change You?|23278674|The Buddha Pill Can Meditation Change You?|Miguel Farias|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1434129769l/23278674._SY75_.jpg|42817278] I learned about the three successive waves of Eastern yogis and teachers coming to the West since 1870. This book focuses on the first two waves and their most prominent protagonists. I found many aspects very interesting, but other parts I skipped.

First Wave: Late 19th to Early 20th Century
* Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902). World Parliament of Religions in Chicago 1893
* Ramana Maharshi (1879-1950). Holy mountain of Arunachala, only a loincloth. Teachings centered on the practice of self-inquiry, summarized in the question "Who am I?". Famous guests included [a:Sommerset Maugham|22259819|Sommerset Maugham|https://s.gr-assets.com/assets/nophoto/user/u_50x66-632230dc9882b4352d753eedf9396530.png] who used him as model for "Sri Ganesha" in [b:The Razor's Edge|31196|The Razor's Edge|W. Somerset Maugham|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1386925123l/31196._SY75_.jpg|2095259]
* Paramahansa Yogananda (1893-1952). Only touched upon in this book. Introduced the West to Kriya Yoga through his book [b:Autobiography of a Yogi|639864|Autobiography of a Yogi|Paramahansa Yogananda|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1347427162l/639864._SY75_.jpg|2066960] and the Self-Realization Fellowship.
* Meher Baba (1894-1969). Declared himself to be an Avatar (direct descent of God). He embraced people from all castes and worked with the poor. He worked with individuals who were considered spiritually advanced but mentally disturbed, whom he referred to as "masts." Later many rich western woman followed him. Since 1925 he maintained a vow of silence.
* Jiddu Krishnamurti (1895-1986). Proclaimed as "Messiah" by the Theosophical Society, but distanced himself from any religious affiliations

Second Wave: Mid 20th Century
* Neem Karoli Baba (~1905-1973). Guru of Ram Dass. Emphasized love, service, devotion, and the remembrance of God.
* Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (1918-2008). Transcendental Meditation (TM). Beatles, All you need is love. Gigantomaniac, believed that a significant number of people practicing TM could positively influence the collective consciousness of society
* Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh / Osho (1931-1990). He emphasized the importance of meditation, awareness, love, free sex, celebration, courage, creativity, and humor. Communes in India, then US, very contoversial, including bioterror attack and collection of 60 Rolls-Royce
* Ram Dass / Richard Alpert (1931-2019). Professor at Harvard, collaborated with Timothy Leary in controversial research on psychedelics, particularly LSD. Transformed to Ram Dass, becoming a beloved spiritual teacher who bridged Eastern and Western spiritual philosophies. [b:Be Here Now|41580312|Be Here Now|Ram Dass|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1535737556l/41580312._SY75_.jpg|29717]

I read the seminal "End of History" from Francis Fukuyama probably some 25 years ago, which argues "that liberal democracy, with its principles of individual freedom, political pluralism, and free-market capitalism, represents the final stage in the development of political ideologies" (summarized by ChatGPT). Obviously we were wrong, and since 10 years pessimists seem to be proven right after every election, Brexit, the rise of illiberal "democracies", etc. Picked up this little book in the hope of glimpsing a way out if this downward spiral. Appreciated Fukuyama's analysis of threats to our liberal democracies from both right and left. Some notes/reminders
* Neo-liberalism is not equal to (classical) liberalism, but an abberation
* Freedom and also protection of free speech is essential, atacks increasing, 3 major threats (authorian states, private tech actors, but also the sheer volume of (mis)information)
* Between national identity and universal liberalism is a powerful point of tension
The book concludes with an updated set of liberal principles and a call for moderation from all actors, OK agreed. But still searching for a drinking straw to rebuild a more optimistic perspective on contemporary politics.

Title: The Buddha Pill: Can Meditation Change You?
Author: Miguel Farias
My Review:
As I practice meditation between 4-6 days per week over the last 10 years, i am naturally curious about any scientific evaluations of its effects. The books overall conclusion is plausible:

* a lot of optimistic biased research on meditation does not hold up to scientific scrutiny
* there is MODERATE scientific evidence that meditation increases emotions, reduces anxiety, etc.
* BUT: unclear how much is attribuable specifically to meditation vs a more general relaxation effect that also arises through 15min of pausing
* meditation can in some (rare) cases also produce negative emotions/effects
* even advanced meditators can be "assholes", meditation alone does not make you a good person - see the Buddha's eightfold path

In particular interesting to me:

* The current wave of Mindfulness is the third meditation wave coming to the West. The first wave was driven by Hindu spiritual leaders such as Vivekananda in the late 1800s or Yogananda in the 1930s. Then in the 1970s Transcendental Meditation (TM) by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi generated huge excitement in the West. Lots of studies on a new state of consciousness, etc. This paved the way for the current and third meditation hype cycle.
* Yogananda and TM come from Hindu traditions, their meditation styles often involve repeating mantras etc. By contrast, the current mindfulness trend has been derived from buddhist tradition. The main technique is to observe your thoughts and thereby detach from its emotions, and ultimately avoid any suffering.
* My personal meditation techniques are definitely rooted in Hindu tradition, in particular trying to concentrate on the third eye and to empty the mind. I have recently tried Buddhist mindfulness and meta techniques again, but do not easily connect. However, I relate to Buddhist philosophy much more then to Hindu religion.
* I was not aware of the thight connection between the 1970s meditation boom and LSD. See Timothly Leary and Ram Dass.

The book also explores in depth the effect of meditation & yoga on prisoners, and whether meditation can replace therapy (of course not) - not very interesting to me. I also found the "anecdotal" writing style excessive. Overall 3 stars.

The marketing splash around the new novel had already reached me in Dec 2021. So when i tested positive for Covid/Omikron in mid of Jan 2022, I reduced my workload and downloaded [b:Anéantir|59839615|Anéantir|Michel Houellebecq|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1643316704l/59839615._SX50_.jpg|94252033] - which became a wonderful quarantine companion!

Strong start involving a mysterious cyber threat, then shifting to the personal and family life of Paul, énarque and advisor to the french economy minister. Paul is probably around my age in the novel (which is set in 2027) and also in many other aspects I can easily relate to him. The novel delves into the relationships of Paul with his parents, sister (cathó) and brother (suicide). The broken marriage with Prudence. The friendship with the minister, the presidential election. Interspersed with many witty and funny elaborations about God(s), the world and The Matrix (and some boring deam sequences).

While all the cynism and nihilsm is still there, I was astonished to see a love story emerging! In an unexpected twist, Prudence and Paul heal their marriage, even their sex gets a romantic touch. Certainly a surprise! As Paul comes to term with his terminal cancer, the novel ends on a sad but beautiful tone.

I feel reconciliated with Houellebecq :)

* Focus on the neocortex, labeled the new brain (vs the 30% old reptilian brain)
* Basic units are cortical columns which act as universal predictors and are trained through feedback loops
* 1.000 columns predict and vote in parallel
* Prediction/understanding requires "reference frames" aka context
Fascinating topic, provocative ideas, very interesting read.

BUT: the author seems over-confident / self-inflating, relying on very few sources besides himself - this triggered my cross-check impulse. After some research (see eg Robert Thibadeau) i think this "theory of intelligence" is rather an additional glimmer on the topic than ground-breaking understanding. And probably many presented ideas are not new in the computational cognitive neuroscience community. Nevertheless intriguing to me!

Part 2 and 3 on AI and human future are a collection of personal viewpoints which i only skimmed through quickly.

Overall I am rather disappointed with Yuval Hararis new oeuvre. It feels less like a book, but rather like a collection of essays (which probably was the starting point). And I think i heard most arguments already before, in his other books, or interviews/talks which I have been following pretty closely over the last 2 years.

Perhaps the title and the 2 previous ambitious books set up the wrong expectations: instead of the anticipated deep insight into whats going on in the 21st century, it is more like a bunch of anecdotes. Some of them very insightful (eg history of fake news), some too shallow (eg the discussion of immigration), some of them too funny. But it is not "explaining" our current state of affairs in the way Sapiens is explaining our history.

The last chapter "Meditation" aroused my particular attention, since I am also meditating daily (at least trying to sit almost every day). Harari launched already in Sapiens the concept of "stories" eg religions, nations, money, etc as basis for human large scale cooperation. He again forcefully dismantles theses stories/illusions in 21 lessons, and I very much agree on this one. Then at the end of the book he cites his meditation experience as the way to go to understand the world and reduce the suffering. This resonates very strongly with me. Nevertheless, in the context of this book, it comes across as a shallow answer to the complex problems we are facing in the 21st century.

Title: Why Buddhism is True: The Science and Philosophy of Meditation and Enlightenment
Author: Robert Wright
My Review:
I highly recommend this book to all my meditating friends! It explains monkey mind, how meditation can help and buddhist insights through modern evolutionary psychology.

My key take-aways:
* the human mind is an evolutionary product of many layers - or rather modules, eg the mating module, the defend myself module, the show off module, etc. Depending on the situation a certain module is in charge, then another and so one. But: there is no managing director/CEO - we are governed by multiple selves rather then one self. The impression of a unique, consistent self is more like an ex-post illusion - a useful one from an evolutionary standpoint.
* When we are at rest, nothing to do, and no module is obviously in charge - the modules compete for attention by bombarding the mind with thoughts - monkey mind!
* Our mind is not designed for happiness, but obviously for evolutionary fitness. Unfortunately never-ending dissatisfaction helped our ancestors get their genes into the next generation
* Meditation: Calming the (monkey) mind through breath techniques is fairly common across traditions. When I come that far, I typically try to do "concentration meditation", in particular opening the 3rd eye or similar. Mindfulness meditation is different, in focusing on your body, thoughts, emotions, paying nonjudgmental attention, not rejecting anything. I am beginning to understand the value of this old Vipassana way of meditation.

Probably some of the claims linking the Buddha to the authors home turf of evolutionary psychology are exaggerated, but nevertheless (and despite the sometimes jokey tone), this book makes a deep impression on me.

My Review:
Great book that I could not put away! Based on very recent technological advances in ancient human genome analysis, the history of modern human evolution is completely rewritten - fascinating! Instead of a "Stammbaum" of human populations, a far more fragmented picture of constantly mixing/interbreeding populations emerges, with stunning surprises on all continents.

The author David Reich, a renowned US geneticist, is also touching upon the historically difficult subject of genetics & racism - while there is almost no research confirming old prejudices, the topic will certainly resurface due to new genetic sampling power. I am concerned about this, let's be prepared for future controversies by understanding the underlying science.

My Review:
Humanity has overcome 3 major challenges: Famine, plague and war

Humanism is "only" a collective myth/religion

• Humanism is a form of religion that worships humankind instead of God. It puts humankind and its desires as a top priority in the world in which humans themselves are framed as the dominant beings. Humanists believe that ethics and values are derived internally within each individual, rather than from an external source
• Modernity: humans give up meaning in return for power
• Technological developments have threatened the continued ability of humans to give meaning to their lives

Fundamente unseres Weltbildes erodieren

• Narrator self vs expiriencing self
• Organisms are algorithms: we are nothing but data-processing machine

Homo Deus: self-made gods

• human nature will be transformed in the 21st century

Title: Ancient Rome: The Rise and Fall of An Empire
Author: Simon Baker
My Review:
Interesting background for any Rome traveller. Covers roman republic + empire.

Focus on 6 key events (e.g. Julius Caesar), delibateraly skipping minor episodes. I liked [a:Simon Baker|83258|Simon Baker|https://s.gr-assets.com/assets/nophoto/user/u_50x66-632230dc9882b4352d753eedf9396530.png]'s ability to put things into a historical, economical, political & technological context. E.g. explaining how the growing empire created social imbalances that favored a new type of politicians and ultimately resulted in a new governance paradigm for the empire. Combined with entertaining stories about the greatest and influential Roman personalities.

Title: When Nietzsche Wept: A Novel Of Obsession
Author: Irvin D. Yalom
My Review:
I read [a:Irvin D. Yalom|909675|Irvin D. Yalom|https://d.gr-assets.com/authors/1238455380p2/909675.jpg]s historical novel a couple of years ago, but recently came across it again. The book resonates with me for many reasons. It is based in Vienna in the 1880's, it's about psychoanalysis and its pioneers [a:Josef Breuer|224700|Josef Breuer|https://d.gr-assets.com/authors/1351701954p2/224700.jpg] and [a:Sigmund Freud|10017|Sigmund Freud|https://d.gr-assets.com/authors/1406688955p2/10017.jpg], i remember an excellent theater evening following Anna O./Bertha Pappenheimers fate, and last but not least like Josef Breuer i am now forty, married and struggling with extensive duties and commitments. Only Nietzsches philosohpy has remained a stranger to me, but all the more intriguing.

Both main characters struggle with despair. Josef Breuer is challenged by Friedrich Nietzsche and defends himself "There is such a thing as a duty to others and I have been faithful to that duty", when F.N. retorts "Duty and faithfulness are shams, curtains to hide behind. Self-liberation means a sacred no, even to duty. You want to become yourself. [...] How often have you lamented that you have never known your freedoom? Your goodness, your duty, your faithfulness - these are the bars of your prison."

Good questions. Although the answer/solution seemed too simplistic. I was almost disappointed when the chapter about Dr. Breuer leaving wife, family and Vienna for the sake of freedom, turned out to be only a 2h dream/hypnosis/trance - but long enough to teach him "Amor fati - love your fate" and to cure him from despair.

Nevertheless a very intriguing book!

Title: Soumission
Author: Michel Houellebecq
My Review:
The new Houellebecq does not catch up with "Les Particules élémentaires". The idea of Islam taking over in France is thought-provoking, and his analysis of European decadence, the identitarian mouvement, etc. are high-lights. But the storyline is artificial and boring, the main character not authentic (why would a 20 year old student fall in love with him?).

Concerning the soumission of Europe to Islam, i also disagree. Europe may be in decline, but its humanist & liberal values are not. I have the impression the islamic societies are on their way to adapt themselves to our modern world, with violent eruptions on their fringes. Ultimately the enlightened humanism will prevail, in the meantime we need to fight extremists, but have no fear from moderate islam.
